entities.rationale: A spreading jihadist insurgency, a military junta and very fast population growth on drought-prone land make prolonged insecurity or famine for most people a real risk. Starting from extreme poverty, near-free essentials by 2100 are a long shot even with superintelligence.

Chronic food shortages, a brittle regime and a nuclear standoff mean war, regime collapse or a repeat of the 1990s famine are serious possibilities. Abundance mostly depends on a peaceful opening or reunification with the South.

Syria is emerging from a civil war with severe hunger, a fragile new government and extreme water stress, so a relapse into conflict or drought-driven crisis is likely enough to dominate. Rebuilding to near-free essentials by 2100 is unlikely.

Jihadist groups already control much of the country and have squeezed the capital, so most Malians losing physical safety for years is close to a coin flip. Climate stress on farming and herding adds famine risk.

A large share of the territory is contested by insurgents and millions are displaced under a military government, making prolonged insecurity for a majority quite likely. Rising water stress threatens food in a very poor economy.

Malawi is peaceful but extremely poor, heavily indebted and dependent on rain-fed maize, so a long climate-driven food crisis is the main danger. Its low starting point makes near-free essentials improbable.

Zambia is stable, but widespread hunger, a debt crisis and drought exposure of both crops and hydropower create a meaningful risk of prolonged food or power loss. Copper wealth helps but is far from enough for abundance.

Good health and full electricity access are offset by crushing debt and heavy reliance on imported fuel, as the 2022 crisis showed, though that crisis was short of a five-year collapse. Middling income gives a modest chance of abundance under superintelligence.

Chad has a long history of civil war, sits between conflicts in Sudan, Libya and the Sahel, and has very weak health, water and food systems. It has the worst readiness to adapt in this group, so abundance is very unlikely.

Kazakhstan is fairly rich, food-secure and an energy exporter, so collapse risk is mostly global doom plus a Russia-related security shock or water shortage. Its wealth gives a reasonable chance of abundance if superintelligence arrives.

Chile has strong institutions, high life expectancy and near-universal services, so its own collapse risk is low apart from severe water stress. It is among the better-placed here for abundance, but near-free essentials still need superintelligence.

More than half the population is already undernourished, the state barely functions and al-Shabaab remains strong, so another long war or drought famine is more likely than not. Abundance is very unlikely from this base.

As an EU and NATO member with high income and stable services, Romania mainly risks global doom or a wider war spilling over from Ukraine. EU-level wealth gives it one of the better shots at abundance under superintelligence.
Senegal is a stable democracy, but a debt crisis, sharply rising water stress and Sahel insurgency on its borders add risk. Low income keeps abundance unlikely.

High violence, weak government and drought in the Dry Corridor threaten security and food, though a nationwide five-year breakdown is not the base case. Middling income gives a small chance of abundance with superintelligence.

Ecuador has good health and electricity access, but gang violence has exploded and drought-hit hydropower has caused blackouts, so security is the main path to collapse. Abundance needs superintelligence and better governance.

Cambodia is growing steadily with low debt, but Mekong flows, climate risk to rice and border tension with Thailand are real vulnerabilities. Its modest income makes abundance unlikely without superintelligence.
Zimbabwe has a record of economic meltdown, hunger and health-system failure under weak governance, and drought threatens its food supply. Low readiness to adapt makes abundance very unlikely.
Military rule, coup risk, a weak health system that buckled under Ebola and an unstable region drive the risk. Plentiful water and minerals help, but abundance from this base is improbable.

Benin is relatively stable, but jihadist violence is spreading into its north from the Sahel, and poverty and weak water and health services limit resilience. Abundance is unlikely without superintelligence.
